analysis.one_liner: Protects doctors and nurses who provide legal abortion, contraception, and IVF care from state interference.
analysis.headline: The bill, which had 30 Democratic and Independent cosponsors in the Senate, was referred to the Judiciary Committee in April 2023 and never received a hearing, vote, or floor action before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: After some states restricted abortion, this bill would make it unlawful for anyone, including a state, to block, punish, or harass doctors, nurses, and pharmacists who provide reproductive health care that is legal where they provide it. It would let the Justice Department, providers, and patients sue to stop state rules that interfere with that care, bar states from using federal money to go after providers, stop malpractice insurers from dropping providers for offering such care, and spend $80 million on legal defense and security grants for clinics and staff.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients seeking abortion, contraception, or IVF services, and the doctors, nurses, midwives, and pharmacists who provide them. The people most directly helped are patients in states where officials have restricted or penalized such care, and providers in any state who face lawsuits, license threats, or harassment for offering care that is legal where they work.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Patients and providers of reproductive care

how_it_helps.text: Bars individuals, entities, and states from preventing or restricting providers from offering reproductive health services that are legal in the state where they are provided, including care for out-of-state patients [S3].
Lets the Attorney General, providers, and patients sue to strike down state rules that interfere, waives state immunity from those suits, and awards attorney's fees to winning plaintiffs [S3].

Prohibits states from using federal funds to pursue legal cases or licensing actions against providers offering legal reproductive care, and bars malpractice insurers from denying coverage or suing providers solely for offering it [S3].

Appropriates $40 million for legal defense grants and $40 million for security grants to clinics that provide or refer for abortion care, covering facility upgrades, staff training, cybersecurity, and patient data protection [S3].

analysis.who_pays: States that restrict abortion would face lawsuits and could have their enforcement rules struck down, and would lose the ability to use federal money for those cases. Malpractice insurers could no longer refuse coverage to providers over these services. The $80 million in grants would come from the Treasury, so taxpayers generally.

drawbacks.text: The bill sweeps a wide range of care under one federal shield, including IVF and counseling, and lets providers sue on behalf of their patients, which raises federalism objections from states that see abortion policy as their own to set [S3].
Its abrogation of state immunity and a nationwide private right of action over any rule affecting care 'that in any way affects commerce' would face serious constitutional challenge in court [S3].

The $80 million in grants funds legal defense for providers facing state enforcement even in states whose voters and legislatures chose those restrictions, a cost an opponent would call federal overreach [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would give real protection to patients and providers where abortion remains legal but providers face lawsuits, license threats, and harassment, and the security and legal-defense grants respond to documented pressure on clinics. The costs are the federalism conflict with states that restrict abortion, roughly $80 million in spending, and real legal vulnerability in its broad abrogation of state immunity. For people who believe legal care should not depend on which state a provider works in, the benefits outweigh the costs; for those who prioritize state control of abortion policy, the same features are the bill's central flaw.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee on the day it was introduced and sat there for the rest of the Congress, with no hearing, no committee vote, and no floor action.

narrative.text: Sen. Patty Murray introduced the bill on April 26, 2023, with 27 original cosponsors, all Democrats or Independents [S3].
It was read twice and referred to the Committee on the Judiciary that same day [S5].
Thirty senators, 29 Democrats and 1 Independent, cosponsored the bill by the end of the Congress [S4].
No further action of any kind appears in the bill's history: no hearing, no markup, no committee report, no floor vote [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: States that restrict abortion and malpractice insurers keep the current rules untouched, since no protections or limits were enacted. Providers and patients seeking these services are no better off than before.

sides.party_line_note: All 30 cosponsors were Democrats or Independents; no Republican cosponsored, and the bill never reached a vote, so the full chamber never took a recorded position.

industries.note: The bill would bar insurers from denying liability coverage to, or suing, providers solely because they offer legal reproductive health care. Insurers currently can decline such providers, and patients lose access when providers cannot get coverage. [S3]

industries.industry: Health care providers (physicians, nurses, midwives, pharmacists)
industries.note: Providers would gain federal protections against state lawsuits, licensing actions, and harassment, plus legal-defense and security funding. Patients benefit alongside providers because protected providers keep offering care. [S3]
States that restrict abortion could no longer enforce those rules against lawful interstate care, would lose immunity from federal suits, and could not use federal funds for enforcement cases. [S3]
